subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that the circles x² + y² − 4x − 6y − 12 = 0 and x² + y² + 6x + 18y + 26 = 0 touch each other. Find the point of contact and the equation of the common tangent at their point of contact.

mark_split.label: Centre and radius of the first circle
Centre and radius of the second circle

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, SENIOR INTER MATHS-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.112 — the Bullet Model Paper, under "Q18 & 19: CIRCLES". It is NOT in the numbered LAQ chapter, so it is authored here as an extra; the book also prints it as a practice box on book p.19 with the answers (1/13, −21/13) and 5x + 12y + 19 = 0 only. Its SECTION follows the paper slot: the Bullet Model Paper places it at Q18/Q19, which is Section C, so it is an LAQ. No appearance tag is printed beside it. The mark split is OURS, not the book’s: this answer sits on a two-column page with no printed margin tags. Star rank: the book gives the CIRCLE LAQ chapter ★★★ in its LAQ chapter table (book p.13), in the chapter header (book p.14) and in the LAQ hit list header (book p.7), so every Circle LAQ entry takes stars 3. That rank belongs to the CHAPTER, not to this question. Paper position: Maths-2B Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Circle holds Q18 and Q19. An LAQ on this paper is 7 marks, never 8 — the 2026-27 move to 8-mark long answers is first year only. WHERE THE BOOK IS WRONG: on book p.112 the second circle is printed as "S′ ≡ x² + y² + 2x − 8y + 13 = 0, Centre C₂ = (−3, −9), radius r₂ = √(1 + 16 − 13) = 2". That equation and that radius line are copied from answer 5.3 on book p.19 and do not belong to this question. The question's own second circle is x² + y² + 6x + 18y + 26 = 0, which gives C₂ = (−3, −9) and r₂ = √(9 + 81 − 26) = √64 = 8 — and the book's very next lines use r₁ + r₂ = 5 + 8 = 13, so 8 is the value it actually needed. The correct equation and radius are written on this card. Everything else was re-derived and is correct. FIGURE SCOPE: the question does not say "draw", so the diagram step carries NO marks. insider_note: The radii here are 5 and 8 and the distance between the centres is exactly 13, so the touching is external — the ratio 5 : 8 is not a round number, which is why the point of contact has thirteenths in it.

steps.label: Centre and radius of the first circle
steps.margin_note: One mark. The constant is negative, so −c adds to g² + f² and the radius is comfortably large.
steps.memory_tip: Centre is (−g, −f); radius is √(g² + f² − c). A negative c makes the radius bigger.
steps.why: Comparing with the general form gives g = −2 and f = −3. Since c = −12, the term −c is +12, which is why the radius comes out as a whole number.
common_mistakes: Subtracting 12 instead of adding it and getting √1.

steps.label: Centre and radius of the second circle
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The book prints the wrong equation here; use the circle the question actually gives.
steps.memory_tip: Halve 6 and 18 to get g = 3 and f = 9, then change both signs for the centre.
steps.why: The book’s printed line "S′ ≡ x² + y² + 2x − 8y + 13 = 0 … r₂ = 2" is copied from a different question and is wrong here. The question’s own circle gives r₂ = 8, which is the value the book’s next line uses when it writes r₁ + r₂ = 5 + 8 = 13.
common_mistakes: Copying the book’s r₂ = 2 and then failing the touching test.
Reading g = 6 and f = 18 without halving.

steps.label: Show that the circles touch
steps.margin_note: Two marks. 5, 12, 13 is a familiar right-triangle triple, so the square root is exact.
steps.memory_tip: 5² + 12² = 13². The distance between the centres works out whole.
lines: ∴ The circles touch each other externally.
steps.why: The distance between the centres equals the sum of the radii, so the circles meet at exactly one point and neither lies inside the other.
common_mistakes: Using r₂ = 2 from the book’s misprint and getting 7 instead of 13.
Writing (3 + 9)² as (3 − 9)², which still gives 144 but by accident.

steps.label: Find the point of contact
steps.margin_note: Two marks. External touching means internal division, in the ratio r₁ : r₂ = 5 : 8.
steps.memory_tip: Ratio 5 : 8 with denominator 13 — the same 13 as the distance between the centres.
lines: P divides C₁C₂ internally in the ratio
steps.why: The contact point is at distance r₁ from C₁ and r₂ from C₂ along the segment joining them, which is internal division in the ratio r₁ : r₂. The denominator 5 + 8 = 13 is why the answer has thirteenths.
common_mistakes: Swapping the centres so that C₂ is multiplied by 8.
Using external division and dividing by 5 − 8 = −3.

steps.label: Find the common tangent
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Take out the factor −2 at the end so the leading coefficient is positive.
steps.memory_tip: Common tangent at the point of contact is S − S′ = 0. Subtract term by term.
lines: The common tangent at the point of contact
steps.why: The x² and y² terms cancel, leaving a straight line that meets both circles only at P. A check: 5(1/13) + 12(−21/13) + 19 = (5 − 252 + 247)/13 = 0, so P lies on it.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as −10x − 24y − 38 = 0 without taking out the factor.

steps.label: The picture
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own; the question does not ask for a diagram. A rough sketch settles internal against external division.
steps.memory_tip: Two circles side by side, touching at one point between the centres.
steps.why: With the circles drawn outside each other, the contact point plainly lies between the centres, which is what makes the internal section formula the right one. The common tangent is at right angles to C₁C₂ through that point.
common_mistakes: Drawing one circle inside the other, which is the internal-touch case.
Drawing the tangent through the midpoint of C₁C₂ instead of through P.
